title: Moving into a rental: what to document first
dek: Record the condition before unpacking, send a clear inventory, and keep proof of delivery alongside your lease, deposit and key records.
metaDescription: Document a rental move-in with room-by-room photos, a condition inventory, written repair requests, deposit records and proof of delivery.

paragraphs: When moving into a rental, document the property's condition before your belongings cover it. Take original photos, complete the required move-in inventory, report existing problems in writing and keep proof you sent it. Photos support a condition checklist; they do not automatically replace a signed form or local submission requirements.

Moving day already has enough decisions. You do not need a professional inspection report to notice a chipped worktop or stained carpet. You do need a record that identifies the room, the defect and when you reported it. This is a US organizing guide, not a statement of every state's rental law.

body.heading: Before the boxes cover the evidence
items: Read the lease and move-in instructions for the inventory form, delivery method and deadline.
Photograph each room in wide view, then photograph existing defects close up.
Include cupboards, appliance interiors, windows, flooring and fixtures where safely accessible.
Write room names and factual descriptions on the inventory; avoid guessing the cause of damage.
Record keys, fobs, access devices and relevant meter readings without publishing access codes.
Send the inventory and repair requests through the required channel and retain the sent copy.
Ask for acknowledgement and a signed copy where applicable; save those separately from your own notes.
Back up original files and store the signed lease, deposit receipt and contact details together.

body.heading: Make photos easy to connect to the inventory
paragraphs: Keep the original files, including their metadata, rather than relying only on a messaging app's compressed copies. A visible date is not essential to the usefulness of a photo; preserve the original and record the inspection date in the inventory. Take a wide shot showing where the defect is, then a close-up showing its detail.

Use simple file names or an index such as Kitchen-01, Kitchen-02 and Hall-01. Describe 'dark mark beside refrigerator, approximately palm-sized' rather than 'landlord's leak damage.' If the cause is unknown, say so. A video walkthrough can add context but can make individual defects harder to locate later.

body.heading: Invented example: a condition record
body.intro: Fictional entries illustrate documentation, not legal conclusions about deductions.
rows: Hall-01 wide; Hall-02 detail; inventory item 4
Two keys and one fob received
Handover list copied; count acknowledged by manager
Extractor does not run using normal switch
Written report sent; no cover removed or wiring inspected

body.heading: Send a condition email with a separate repair request

items.line: I collected keys for [address] on [date]. Attached is my move-in condition inventory with indexed photos. Please confirm receipt and send a signed copy if that is part of the process. These entries record the condition I observed before unpacking.

The bathroom extractor did not operate using its normal switch on [date]. I have attached the relevant inventory entry. Please confirm how to report this formally, the next step and any access arrangements needed.

body.heading: Save the financial and date records too
paragraphs: Keep the deposit amount, payment receipt, payee and any required protection or holding information. Record the lease start and end, any renewal process, and notice requirements from the actual lease and applicable local rules. Do not copy another tenant's notice period into your calendar.

The [California Department of Real Estate guide](https://www.dre.ca.gov/publications/ResourceGuidebook/gb07_when.html) discusses rental agreement terms and pre-move-in inspection records. Its California-specific rules are not national rules. For help finding the relevant agency or legal assistance where you rent, use [USAGov's tenant-rights page](https://www.usa.gov/tenant-rights).

body.heading: When documenting is not enough
paragraphs: A dangerous condition is not a photography assignment. If there is an immediate threat, leave the unsafe area and contact the appropriate emergency service or utility. Do not touch exposed wiring, dismantle appliances or investigate a suspected gas leak to get better evidence.

If the manager refuses to acknowledge the inventory, keep the sent record and seek local advice about the correct notice procedure. Do not assume silence means agreement. Likewise, do not withhold rent or pay for repairs expecting reimbursement without checking the law and procedure that apply to your tenancy.

Wear, damage, cleaning charges and deposit return deadlines depend on local law and the facts. A record helps describe and challenge a claim; it does not guarantee a particular result. At move-out, repeat the same room sequence so the two records can be compared.

items.q: Are photos enough without a signed checklist?
items.a: Do not assume so. Photos are useful supporting evidence, but your lease or local law may require a particular inventory, signature or submission process. Complete that process and keep a copy. Ask for acknowledgement of delivery even if the landlord has not agreed with every observation.

items.q: What if I notice damage after unpacking?
items.a: Record it as soon as you notice it, with the actual discovery date and any relevant earlier photo. Report it in writing through the required channel. Do not alter dates or describe it as definitely pre-existing if you are unsure; explain what you know and what you cannot establish.

items.q: Should I label marks as normal wear and tear?
items.a: Describe the condition first. Whether it counts as ordinary wear or chargeable damage depends on local rules and circumstances, including the item's condition and use. An exact observation and a linked photo are more useful than a confident legal label that may be wrong.

visuals.title: Record, send, preserve

steps.label: Observe
steps.detail: Take a wide room view and a close-up of each existing defect.

steps.label: Index
steps.detail: Connect each photo to a room and condition-inventory entry.

steps.label: Deliver
steps.detail: Use the required reporting channel and keep the sent record.

steps.label: Retain
steps.detail: Back up originals and any acknowledgement or signed copy.

visuals.caption: Photos support the required inventory rather than replacing its local process.
visuals.alt: Four steps connect move-in observations to indexed photos, delivered inventory and preserved original evidence.

visuals.title: Receipt is not agreement

steps.label: Your observation
steps.detail: The inventory says what you saw at move-in.

steps.label: Delivery record
steps.detail: A sent message or receipt shows when the inventory was delivered.

steps.label: Response
steps.detail: A signed copy or reply records what the landlord actually acknowledged or agreed.

visuals.caption: Do not treat a missing reply as agreement about the condition.
visuals.alt: Observation, delivery evidence and the landlord's response are shown as distinct rental documentation records.

research.primaryQuery: moving into a rental what to document
